title: Caring for elders
hookLine: looking after ageing parents as seva
tomorrow: Simran drives Bebe to therapy. then a truck cuts her off.

lines: HER ROOM, OR A REHAB STAY?
cards: Bebe Jaswant went out to check her chilies, caught her foot on the hose, and now her ankle is wrapped and propped on two pillows. The doctor says weeks, not days, and no stairs. Bebe's house has stairs.
That night the family talks it over at the kitchen table. Simran's dad wants Bebe to stay in Simran's room while she heals.

Bhua Kiran wonders if Bebe would rather have a short stay at a rehab place, with nurses and her own routine. And Simran asks the question underneath it: if we look after Bebe, is that seva? Or is it just what family does?

teach.b: Sikhs answer that question two ways, and both have a point.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: SEVA IS THE HEART.
teach.b: The first view: seva is selfless service, done for others with no claim on you and nothing owed back.
Caring for your own grandmother is a duty, a beautiful one, but calling it seva can stretch the word until it means everything.
Its best case: it keeps seva pointed outward, at the stranger, the hungry, the one nobody's responsible for. The second view: the word is about the heart, not the address.
Service without ego, without keeping score, is seva wherever it happens, and an elder's room may be the hardest place to serve without keeping score.
Its best case: if seva only counts at the gurdwara, home becomes the place where we're tired and short.
Guru Nanak, on ang 26, says in paraphrase: serve in this world, and you'll be given a seat in the Lord's court. In this world, he says. He doesn't name the room.

teach.h: HOME, OR GOOD CARE AND VISITS.
teach.b: Families also weigh the practical side: some care at home, some find good care elsewhere and visit often, and both can be done with love.

By the end of dinner, Simran's family has chosen: her room, for now, and a nurse friend of Bhua Kiran's will check in. Simran carries her desk into the hall, and Bebe, from the couch, tells her exactly where it goes.

how: Many Sikh families care for elders at home, often across generations under one roof, while others arrange outside care and visit; seva is understood as service done without ego.

o: leaving elders' care entirely to doctors and nurses
a ceremony honoring grandparents once a year
looking after older family as service, at home or nearby

games.q: two views, one table — tap the pairs.
p: seva is the heart, at any address
serve in this world, find a seat
her room, for now, plus a nurse

s: seva only counts when it's done at a gurdwara
that's one side of a real debate; Guru Nanak on ang 26 says serve in this world and doesn't name the room.
some Sikhs say caring for your own family is duty, and keep the word seva for strangers
its best case: it keeps seva pointed outward, at the one nobody's responsible for.
the Guru Granth Sahib requires that elders always live with their children
the lesson names no such rule; families care at home or arrange good care and visit, and both can be done with love.

games.q: your aunt says looking after grandpa is just family duty, not seva. your dad says it's the realest seva there is. what's the best case for your aunt's side?
o: it keeps seva pointed outward, at the people nobody owes anything.
family care matters less than serving at the gurdwara.
grandpa shouldn't need help if the family raised him right.
games.why: that's the first view's best case. the second view's: if seva only counts at the gurdwara, home becomes the place where we're tired and short.

practice: Bring to mind one older person in your life. Name one thing that's become hard for them, stairs, a form, a phone, an empty afternoon, and picture one small help you could offer, and when. Let that plan settle, and breathe slowly.

wordCard.voice: Caring for elders. Looking after the ones who looked after us, which some Sikhs call seva without leaving the house.

carryVoice: Seva at home: the Guru said serve in this world, and didn't name the room. Back tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 26 (Sri Rag, Mahala 1: vich duniaa sev kamaaeeai taa dargah baisan paaeeai), paraphrased
Sikh practice: seva as service without ego; care of elders in Sikh families, described
